hints.content:
When we have an integral of a sum of functions, we can always split it into the sum of the integrals of each function:

$\displaystyle \int_{3}^6 [f(x)+h(x)] \, dx =\int_{3}^6 f(x) \, dx+\int_{3}^6 h(x) \, dx$

$\displaystyle \int_{3}^6 f(x)\,dx$ is the net area between $y=f(x)$ and the $x$-axis from $x=3$ to $x=6$.

![Function f is graphed. The x-axis goes from negative 7 to 6. The graph consists of a smooth curve. The curve starts at (3, 0), moves downward to a relative minimum in quadrant 4, moves upward and ends at (6, 0). The region above the curve and below the x-axis between x-intercepts 3 and 6 has area negative 6.](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/03418be23c4fe715c5fb0e416cfae8f36b66dd63)

From the graph:

$\displaystyle\int_{3}^6 f(x)\,dx=-6$

$\displaystyle \int_{3}^6 h(x)\,dx$ is the net area between $y=h(x)$ and the $x$-axis from $x=3$ to $x=6$.

![Function h is graphed. The x-axis goes from negative 7 to 6. The graph consists of a smooth curve. The curve starts at (3, 0), moves downward to a relative minimum in quadrant 4, moves upward and ends at (6, 0). The region above the curve and below the x-axis between x-intercepts 3 and 6 has area negative 2.](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/7d41b6d55961ee062883f64c9c58a25f42f40748)

From the graph:

$\displaystyle\int_{3}^6 h(x)\,dx=-2$

Now we can sum up the two integrals:

$\begin{align}
&\phantom{=}\displaystyle \int_{3}^6 [f(x)+h(x)] \, dx
\\\\
&=\displaystyle \int_{3}^6 f(x) \, dx+\int_{3}^6 h(x) \, dx
\\\\
&=-6+(-2)
\\\\
&=-8
\end{align}$
